title: Agency or principal: the question that decides whether marketplace revenue is gross or net
content: Before any marketplace fee can be recognised, one question decides the presentation of every one of them: is the company the principal in the underlying transaction, or an agent arranging it. The principal controls the good or service before it transfers to the customer, bears the inventory and fulfilment risk, and sets the price; it reports the whole contract value as revenue and the supplier's share as a cost. The agent arranges the transaction between two other parties and reports only its own fee as revenue. QuotesDone connects a customer to suppliers who then contract and deliver directly, and the company's chart of accounts is built on that reading: the revenue accounts are Reveal Fee Revenue, Supplier Commission Revenue and Supplier Registration Revenue, all of which are the company's own fees, with no account for supplier contract value passing through. That is the net, agent presentation. If the commercial model ever changes so that the company holds customer funds for the supplier's work or takes delivery risk, this conclusion must be re-assessed before the accounts are prepared, because it changes reported revenue by an order of magnitude without changing profit by anything.

principal_indicators: controls the good or service before transfer
agent_indicators: arranges a transaction between two other parties
structured_data.current_reading: agent, net presentation, evidenced by a chart of accounts with no supplier contract value account
re_assess_if: the company holds customer funds for supplier work
the company takes delivery or performance risk

title: The five-step model for recognising revenue from a contract
content: The framework most reporting regimes now use asks five questions in order. Identify the contract with the customer. Identify the distinct performance obligations in it. Determine the transaction price, including any variable consideration. Allocate that price across the obligations. Recognise revenue as each obligation is satisfied, either at a point in time or over time. The step that decides most marketplace cases is the second: what exactly did the customer buy. If the fee buys a single event, such as being given a supplier's contact details, the obligation is satisfied at that event and revenue is recognised then. If the fee buys access across a period, the obligation is satisfied across that period and revenue is spread. This record describes the shape of the model rather than quoting any standard's text; the standard that applies to this entity and its current wording must be resolved from the applicable financial reporting framework before it is relied on in published statements.

steps: allocate the price to the obligations
recognise as each obligation is satisfied
structured_data.decisive_step_for_a_marketplace: what the fee actually buys, which fixes point-in-time versus over-time
structured_data.resolve_elsewhere: which framework applies to this entity and the current wording of the standard

title: Recognising the reveal fee: the obligation is satisfied at the reveal
content: The reveal fee is charged when a customer is given the identity and contact details of a shortlisted supplier. The performance obligation is that disclosure, and it is satisfied at a single identifiable moment, so revenue is recognised at the reveal rather than when the customer later contracts with the supplier and not when the money settles. The entry is a debit to the clearing or receivable account for the gross amount and a credit to 4000 Reveal Fee Revenue; the processor fee is a separate expense to 6100 and is never netted off. The rate applied is not recorded in this knowledge body: it is held in the platform's own pricing configuration, and the accountant reads it from there for the transaction in question rather than from memory, because a rate that is copied into a knowledge record is a rate that will still be quoted after it changes.

structured_data.obligation: disclosure of supplier identity and contact details
structured_data.recognised: at the reveal event, not at contracting and not at settlement
structured_data.entry: Dr 1050 Stripe Clearing or 1100 AR / Cr 4000 Reveal Fee Revenue
structured_data.rate_source: the platform's pricing configuration, read per transaction; deliberately not stored here

title: Recognising supplier commission, and the receivable that makes it collectable
content: Supplier commission is earned when the event the commission is contingent on has occurred, and it is recognised then rather than when the supplier pays. The entry debits 1110 Supplier Commission Receivable and credits 4100 Supplier Commission Revenue; collection later debits cash and credits 1110. The reason commission gets its own receivable account separate from 1100 Accounts Receivable is that its collection behaviour is different: it is owed by a counterparty who is also a platform participant, so an ageing balance in 1110 is simultaneously a finance problem and a supplier-relationship signal, and mixing it into general receivables hides both. Commission that is contingent on an outcome that has not yet occurred is not revenue and not a receivable; it is not recorded at all until the contingency resolves.

structured_data.recognised: when the contingent event occurs, not when the supplier pays
structured_data.entry: Dr 1110 Supplier Commission Receivable / Cr 4100 Supplier Commission Revenue
structured_data.why_separate_account: commission ageing is a supplier-relationship signal as well as a finance one

title: The supplier registration fee: a single event, or access across a period?
content: A registration fee is recognised according to what it buys, and the two possibilities give different answers. If it pays for a one-off act of onboarding and verification, the obligation is satisfied when that act completes and the whole fee is revenue then, credited to 4200 Supplier Registration Revenue. If it pays for continued listing or access over a term, the obligation is satisfied across that term, so the receipt is credited to 2400 Deferred Revenue and released to 4200 over the period. The determination is made from the terms the supplier actually agreed to and is documented, not assumed from the fee's name; and if the terms are ambiguous the ambiguity is reported rather than resolved in whichever direction flatters the period. The same question recurs whenever a new fee is introduced.

structured_data.if_one_off_onboarding: Dr cash / Cr 4200 Supplier Registration Revenue at completion
structured_data.if_access_over_a_term: Dr cash / Cr 2400 Deferred Revenue, released to 4200 across the term
structured_data.determined_from: the terms the supplier agreed, documented; never assumed from the fee's name

title: Why late-payment and non-response charges sit in their own revenue account
content: Account 4400 Late Payment Fines & Interest carries non-response fines, late interest and administrative fees recovered from suppliers, and it is deliberately separate from 4100 Supplier Commission Revenue. Two reasons. Operationally, the commission receivable must clear to exactly the commission that was billed; a fine mixed into the same account leaves a residue that looks like a collection failure. Analytically, penalty income and commission income behave in opposite directions: commission rising is the marketplace working, penalty income rising is the marketplace failing, and a combined revenue line that grows can hide the second inside the first. A charge of this kind is recognised when it becomes enforceable under the published terms and collectable in the ordinary sense, not at the moment it is theoretically incurred.

structured_data.analytical_reason: commission growth and penalty growth mean opposite things

title: How a refund reverses, and the two things it does not reverse
content: A refund unwinds the revenue and returns the cash, and it is recorded as its own event rather than by amending the original sale. When the refund is agreed but not yet paid, debit the revenue account originally credited, or 6900 Refunds & Bad Debt where the policy is to report refunds as a cost rather than as negative revenue, and credit 2300 Customer Refunds Payable. When it is paid, debit 2300 and credit cash or the clearing account. Two things do not automatically reverse. The processor's fee on the original transaction is frequently not returned, so 6100 stays charged unless the processor's own record shows otherwise. And any commission already recognised on the underlying transaction only reverses if the commission itself is being reversed, which is a separate determination. Choosing between the negative-revenue and the expense presentation is a policy decision that is made once and applied consistently, because switching between them between periods makes the revenue trend meaningless.

structured_data.on_agreement: Dr 4xxx revenue or 6900 Refunds & Bad Debt / Cr 2300 Customer Refunds Payable
structured_data.on_payment: Dr 2300 Customer Refunds Payable / Cr 1000 or 1050
does_not_auto_reverse: the processor fee already charged to 6100
commission recognised on the underlying transaction
structured_data.policy: negative revenue or expense presentation, chosen once and applied consistently

title: The accountant does not approve a refund; the CEO does
content: A refund is a financial matter and the accountant seat owns recording it, reconciling it and reporting it. It does not own approving it. The founder's ruling of 9 September 2026 places approval of refunds, and approval of advertising spend, with the CEO seat, and the standing grants express that as a routing rather than a permission: the grant exists so that the ruling is visible in the table rather than inferred from an absence, and its ceiling is set so that every amount routes to the CEO. In practice this means the accountant may determine that a refund is due under the published policy, may compute the amount, and may prepare the entries, and must then hand the decision on. Posting a refund that was not approved is not a bookkeeping shortcut; it is the seat exercising an authority it was explicitly not given.

owned_by_the_accountant: determining a refund is due under published policy

title: A chargeback is not a refund, and it is recorded differently
content: A refund is initiated by the company; a chargeback is initiated by the cardholder through their bank and imposed on the company, usually with a fee and always with a dispute process. The accounting difference that matters is timing and certainty: a refund is known when it is agreed, whereas a chargeback creates a contingent outflow while the dispute is open and a settled one only when it resolves. So a chargeback is recorded when the funds are actually withdrawn by the processor, with the associated dispute fee charged to 6100 Payment Processing Fees, and a chargeback that is subsequently won is recorded as a recovery event rather than by deleting the original. Counting chargebacks in the same figure as refunds hides a signal, because a rising refund rate is a product or expectation problem and a rising chargeback rate is a trust or fraud problem.

structured_data.chargeback: cardholder-initiated, recorded when funds are withdrawn, dispute fee to 6100
structured_data.if_won: record as a recovery event; never delete the original
structured_data.reporting: track separately from refunds; they signal different problems

title: Partial refunds and credit notes
content: A partial refund reverses part of a transaction and leaves the rest standing, so it must reference the original transaction and state the portion being reversed; a partial refund recorded as a standalone negative amount cannot later be reconciled to the sale it belongs to. Where the amount is credited against future amounts owed rather than returned in cash, the instrument is a credit note: it reduces the receivable rather than moving cash, and it stays outstanding until it is either applied or expires. The discipline in both cases is that the total reversed across all partial refunds and credit notes for one transaction can never exceed the transaction, which is a constraint that should be enforced where the records are written rather than checked afterwards in a report.

structured_data.partial_refund: references the original transaction and states the portion reversed
structured_data.credit_note: reduces a receivable rather than moving cash; tracked until applied or expired
structured_data.invariant: total reversed for a transaction never exceeds the transaction

title: What makes a receipt from the expenses inbox postable
content: Expenses arrive at the expenses mailbox, and an email is not yet an expense. A postable receipt establishes five things: who was paid, what for, how much and in what currency, on what date, and evidence that the payment was made or is owed. A message that names an amount without a supplier, or a supplier without an amount, is held and the missing element is chased. A renewal notice is not a receipt because it says what will be charged rather than what was. Where the document is an attachment, the attachment is the evidence and it is retained addressably, because a posted figure whose only support was the body text of an email that has since been deleted is a figure with no audit trail. Anything that cannot be established is recorded as missing rather than inferred from the supplier's usual behaviour.

required: evidence of payment or of the obligation
structured_data.retention: the attachment is the evidence and is retained addressably

title: Classifying an expense against the chart of accounts
content: Classification maps a receipt to one account code, and the estate holds a category-to-account map in public.gl_expense_map for the recurring cases. The map is a shortcut for known categories, not an authority: a receipt whose category is present in the map is posted to the mapped code, and a receipt whose category is absent is classified on its substance and, if the category will recur, the map is extended deliberately rather than the receipt being forced into the nearest existing category. Classification is decided by what the cost is for rather than by who issued it: a payment to a software vendor for advertising credit is advertising, and a payment to an advertising platform for a data export is not. The test of a classification scheme is whether two similar costs incurred three months apart land in the same account, and the way to make that true is to record the reasoning the first time.

structured_data.map_status: a shortcut for known categories, not an authority
structured_data.decided_by: what the cost is for, not who issued the document

title: Capital or revenue: whether a cost is an expense or an asset
content: A cost that is consumed within the period is an expense and hits the income statement immediately. A cost that creates a resource the company will use across several periods is capital expenditure, and it goes to the balance sheet to be depreciated or amortised over the periods that benefit. Getting this wrong in either direction distorts both statements: expensing an asset understates this period's result and overstates every later one, and capitalising a running cost flatters the current period and leaves a balance that will never legitimately unwind. Recurring subscription software is generally consumed as it is used and is an expense; a one-off purchase of durable equipment is generally capital. The capitalisation threshold below which the company expenses small items regardless, and the treatment of internally developed software, are policy decisions that must be set and recorded rather than decided per invoice.

structured_data.capital: creates a resource used across several periods
structured_data.distortion_if_wrong: in both directions, and it persists across every later period

title: Recording a cost incurred in a currency the books are not kept in
content: The books are kept in one presentation currency and a cost incurred in another is translated into it. The translation uses a rate as at the transaction date rather than the date the receipt was read or the date the report is run, and the rate used, its source and its date are recorded alongside the entry so that the figure can be reproduced. Where the payment settles later at a different rate, the difference between the amount recorded and the amount paid is a foreign exchange gain or loss and belongs in the period it arose in, not in the cost line, because burying it there makes the underlying cost look like it changed when only the rate did. Which rate source the company uses must be chosen once and applied consistently; this record does not name one, and it does not carry any rate.

structured_data.translate_at: a rate as at the transaction date
structured_data.on_settlement_difference: an FX gain or loss in the period it arose, never absorbed into the cost line
not_recorded_here: which rate source the company uses

title: A recurring subscription billed annually is not an annual expense
content: An annual subscription paid once creates a cost that belongs to twelve periods, and it is handled as a prepayment: capitalised to 1400 Prepaid Expenses on payment and released to the relevant expense account across the term. The reason this matters more than it appears is comparability: a monthly cost line that jumps every time an annual tool renews cannot be compared month to month, cannot be used to compute a run rate, and will produce a runway figure that is wrong in whichever direction the renewal calendar happens to fall. For a company whose largest cost category is tooling, the difference between the cash view and the accrual view of software cost is one of the larger reconciling items in any month, and it is worth reporting both rather than choosing between them.

structured_data.treatment: prepayment: Dr 1400 on payment, released to expense across the term
structured_data.why: an unspread annual renewal makes monthly cost incomparable and any run rate wrong
structured_data.reporting: report the cash view and the accrual view of software cost, not one of them

title: Advertising spend: recognised as consumed, approved by the CEO
content: Advertising spend is an operating expense charged to 6200 Marketing & Advertising, and it is recognised as the advertising is delivered rather than when a balance is topped up. A prepaid advertising balance is an asset until it is consumed: money loaded onto a platform account and not yet spent belongs in 1400 Prepaid Expenses, and the amount actually delivered in the period is what reaches 6200. Reading the platform's own reported spend for the period is what measures this, and where the platform's figure and the amount charged to the card differ, both are recorded and the difference is explained rather than averaged. Approval of advertising spend is not the accountant's: the founder's ruling of 9 September 2026 routes it to the CEO, and the accountant's role is to record it, measure its return alongside the revenue it is claimed to have produced, and report both.

structured_data.recognised: as delivered, not when a balance is topped up
structured_data.approval: CEO, per the founder's ruling of 9 September 2026
structured_data.on_a_difference: record both figures and explain the difference; never average them

title: Owner and related-party amounts are identified, never absorbed
content: A cost paid personally by the owner on the company's behalf, a company payment for something personal, and any transaction with a party connected to the owner, are all related-party items. They are recorded like any other transaction and they are additionally identified as related-party, because their significance comes from who they are with rather than from their size, and materiality thresholds do not apply to them. The mechanics are ordinary: an owner-funded cost debits the expense and credits owner capital or a director's account rather than cash; a personal cost paid by the company is not an expense at all and is treated as a distribution or a receivable from the owner. What must never happen is that such an item is classified into a general expense account because it resembles one, since that removes the very fact that made it worth identifying. Any disclosure obligation attaching to related-party transactions is resolved from the applicable reporting framework and the current authority.

structured_data.owner_funded_company_cost: Dr expense / Cr 3000 Owner Capital or a director's account
structured_data.company_paid_personal_cost: not an expense; a distribution or a receivable from the owner
structured_data.rule: identified as related-party regardless of size; materiality does not apply

title: What the accountant does with a receipt it cannot classify
content: An unclassifiable receipt is held, and the holding is itself recorded: the document, what is known about it, what is missing, and who is being asked. It is not posted to General & Administrative because that account is where unclassifiable costs go to become invisible, and a 6300 balance that grows faster than the categories around it is usually not a general administrative cost at all but a classification backlog wearing an account code. The chase has a named next step and a date. If the information cannot be obtained, the item is reported as unclassified with its amount, so that the reader of the period's numbers knows both the size of what is unexplained and that it is unexplained, which is strictly more information than a plausible classification would have given them.

on_unclassifiable: record the document, what is known, what is missing, who is being asked
set a named next step and a date
structured_data.if_never_resolved: report as unclassified with its amount
